title: Zeno's shipwreck
hook: a merchant loses his cargo of purple dye off Athens and wanders into a bookshop
carry: I sailed well when I was wrecked

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus goes free, and opens a school no emperor could close. Your line was the school is inside. What did you write down that no one can take? Day twenty-five.
screen: `EPICTETUS GOES FREE — THE SCHOOL IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: We've met two Stoics: an emperor and an enslaved teacher. Today, the man who started it all, centuries before either of them. His name was Zeno, from Citium, a city on the island of Cyprus. He was a merchant, carrying a cargo of purple dye from Phoenicia. And somewhere off the coast near Athens, the ship went down. The cargo, the fortune, gone into the sea. Zeno made it to shore with, as far as we know, nothing.
screen: `THE MAN WHO STARTED IT ALL.` → `A CARGO OF PURPLE DYE.` → `THE SHIP GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Our source for this is Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote lives of the Greek philosophers centuries after Zeno, collecting stories from older books, some of them already disagreeing. So think of this as the story the ancient world told about Zeno, not a court record. Here's how it goes. Shipwrecked, broke, around thirty years old, Zeno walks up from the harbor into Athens. He doesn't know anyone. He wanders into a bookseller's shop and sits down. And the bookseller is reading aloud, or Zeno picks up, a book about Socrates, written by one of Socrates's students. Zeno is hooked. Something in the way Socrates lived, questioning everything, owning almost nothing, unafraid, hits him right in the chest. He's lost everything he owned, and on the same trip, he finds the thing he'll spend the rest of his life on. Years later, according to Diogenes, Zeno looked back on the wreck and said something like: I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked. Another version has him thanking Fortune for driving him to philosophy. Either way, the man who lost a fortune at sea went on to found a school that would reach an emperor in his tent, an enslaved teacher in Nicopolis, and people reading the Stoics on their phones today. Now, gently. Not every loss sends you somewhere good, and nobody should tell a grieving person that everything happens for a reason. The Stoics didn't say the wreck was good. They said what you do after the wreck is still yours. Zeno's cargo sank. Zeno walked into a bookshop.
screen: `A STORY TOLD CENTURIES LATER.` · `BROKE, IN A BOOKSHOP.` · `A BOOK ABOUT SOCRATES.` · `NOT EVERY LOSS IS A GIFT.` · then, large: `I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then look back over your life for one loss that, in the end, sent you somewhere good. A job that ended. A plan that fell through. A move you didn't want. Not the worst loss, just one where you can see the bookshop now. Let it come back: what sank, and where you washed up. Notice the thread between them. If no loss like that comes, that's all right. Just rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Zeno's shipwreck. A merchant loses his fortune at sea, walks into a bookshop, and finds his life's work.
Your line: I sailed well when I was wrecked. Today, tell someone about the loss that sent you somewhere good. Or just say the line to yourself. Day twenty-five.

howItsDone: Stoics practice looking at a setback as material to work with rather than simply a disaster, asking what response is still in their power after the loss.

fork.setup: you're Zeno. your ship has sunk with everything you own, and you've washed up near Athens knowing no one. where do you end up?
options: in a bookshop, reading about Socrates.
fork.reveal: he wanders into a bookseller's shop and finds a book about Socrates. he later said he made a good voyage when he was shipwrecked.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about losing money.
what it means: a loss that sent a man to the work of his life, and a reminder that what you do after the wreck is yours.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 7.2–5 gives several versions: a shipwreck near the Piraeus, Xenophon's Memorabilia in the shop, and more than one wording of the saying.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.2–5

notes: DL 7.2–5: Zeno wrecked near the Piraeus with a cargo of purple from Phoenicia, about thirty years old; sat in a bookseller's shop reading (or hearing read) Xenophon's Memorabilia book 2. Script says 'a book about Socrates, written by one of Socrates's students'. Confirm.

The saying: DL 7.4 ('I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck', Yonge/Hicks wording varies) and 7.5 (another version, thanking fortune for driving him to philosophy). Paraphrased; the carry is the index's wording.
Dating: Zeno c. 334–262 BCE; Diogenes Laërtius c. 3rd century CE ('about five hundred years after'); Epictetus/Marcus 1st–2nd century CE ('about four hundred years before either'). Confirm.
The script says gently that not every loss is a gift and avoids 'everything happens for a reason'.

Review 2026-10-01: removed the 'four hundred' and 'five hundred years' counts and the 'one of the most expensive goods' superlative (not in Diogenes Laërtius), in the hook, teach, screen and myth; 'in the same week' (invented) became 'on the same trip'; the claim about shaping 'Roman emperors, early Christian writers' now points only to the Stoics already met on this path.
